NYC Capital Forecasts

Budget growth and schedule slippage on New York City capital projects, forecast from public NYC Open Data. City reports from May 2023 to May 2026 (three a year). Every forecast uses only data available at its forecast date, and every result below is from projects held out of training.

What the held-out data show

Schedule slippage is partly predictable and the models beat "the date holds" by a clear margin. Budget growth is mostly not predictable as a number, but the chance of a large increase is. Uncertainty ranges were honest for budgets and too narrow for schedules.

Reading the results

  • Schedule. Open projects' forecast completion dates moved a median 133 days later over the next 12 months in the test period. Gradient boosting cut error by 16.0% versus assuming no move.
  • Budget. 45% of test budget lines did not change at all, so "no change" is hard to beat. The planned-budget number here is the city's plan, not final cost.
  • Uncertainty. The slip rate drifted between the calibration and test periods, so 80% ranges for schedule covered 72%. Drift matters more than the interval method.
  • Completion. A project's own forecast date already ranks near-term completions well (AUC 0.85). Gradient boosting adds +0.015 (95% CI -0.003 to +0.033), which is not a significant gain.

Test = the last two reports with a 12-month outcome (Jan and May 2025 forecasts). 95% intervals: 1,000 bootstrap resamples of projects.

Schedule: how far completion dates slip in 12 months

For each open project, the target is how many days its forecast completion date moves over the next three city reports (about 12 months). If a project finishes, its actual completion date is used. 2,702 project-reports were held out.

Prediction ranges

An 80% range should contain the true outcome for about 80% of projects. For budgets it does. For schedules it does not, because slippage rose after the calibration period.

Budget: change in planned budget over 12 months

The target is the change in a budget line's total planned budget between one city report and the one three reports later (12 months). Spending is only recorded for past fiscal years and the public files do not hold the original approved budget, so this measures plan growth, not final cost overrun. 9,248 budget-line reports from 4,813 lines were held out.

Risk of a large increase

Predicting the size of a change barely beats "no change". Predicting whether a budget line rises by 10% or more works much better.

This classifier was added after the point forecasts showed almost no skill. It is reported whatever it shows.

Completion: survival analysis

2,376 of 3,123 projects are still open when the data ends. Dropping them would make projects look faster than they are, so Kaplan-Meier treats them as censored at their last report. Time counts reports since a project first appeared as open, about four months each.

About 9.5% complete within 12 months and 31% within 36 months. Completion rates differ widely by agency.

Will it complete in the next 12 months?

113 of 2,714 test project-reports completed. The agency's own forecast date is already a strong ranker. Learned models add little, and the simpler models are miscalibrated because completion rates fell between training and test.

What the models rely on

Permutation importance shows how much worse a model gets when one feature is shuffled. Partial dependence shows the model's average prediction as one feature changes. They describe the models, not causes.

  • Schedule: how soon the forecast date is, the project phase and the agency matter most. Projects at or past their date slip the most. Earlier delays add little once those are known.
  • Large budget increase: spending relative to budget, the agency and the size of the budget matter most. The pattern with size is not monotonic.

Method and limits

Data

DatasetRowsCoversContents
Budget and Spend by Fiscal Year288,4468,434 budget linesPlanned budget by fiscal year at each report; spending for past years
Schedule History and Variance22,4643,661 projectsForecast or actual completion date at each report, phase, reason for change
Capital Project Schedules and Budgets14,0694,191 completed phasesSchool-construction phases: planned and actual dates, budget and final estimate
  • 3,916 budget rows with no amount were dropped; 17,755 rows hold negative adjustments and were kept.
  • 3 completion dates with impossible years were set to missing; 5,308 schedule rows have no forecast date.
  • In 8,557 school-phase rows the planned-end field holds a program label rather than a date.

Design

  • Each project at each report is one row. Features use only reports up to that date.
  • Models train on older reports, calibrate on a newer one and test on the last two reports that have a 12-month outcome. A unit test checks that every training label was known at the test date.
  • Models: "no change" and agency-median baselines, an L1-penalized median regression, and gradient boosting. Hyperparameters were fixed in advance.
  • Intervals: conformalized quantile regression (named primary before the test run) and split conformal.

School-construction phases (descriptive only)

Only completed phases are observed, so long phases still open are missing, and many programs have no planned-end date. No forecast is made from this file.

Limitations and analysis log

  • Budget growth is not final cost overrun. The cost target is the change in each project's total planned budget between city reports. Spending is only recorded for past fiscal years, and the public files do not contain the original approved budget. Planned amounts also move between fiscal years as the planning window rolls forward.
  • Short history. There are 10 reports (3 years). Only the last two forecast origins (reports of Jan and May 2025) are held out, and the same projects appear in both, so results come from two correlated test windows. Bootstrap confidence intervals resample projects, not time.
  • Drift. The median 12-month slip changed from 0 to 150 days across origins. Models trained on older reports therefore under-predict recent slippage, and conformal intervals (which assume exchangeable data) under-cover for schedule.
  • Projects that vanish. About 15% of cost rows and 12% of schedule rows disappear from later reports without a completion record. They cannot be labelled, so they are excluded; the results describe projects that stay in the reports.
  • Self-reported data. Agencies report their own forecasts; the NYC Comptroller and State Comptroller have criticised the quality of public capital data. Nothing here is audited.
  • School-construction phases are described only. Completed phases are a biased sample (long phases are still open), and 'planned end' is missing or not a date for many programmes, so no forecasting claim is made from that file.
  • Drivers are associations, not causes. Permutation importance and partial dependence show what the models use, not what causes delay or cost growth.
  • Analysis log. Hyperparameters were fixed in advance and never tuned. The large-budget-increase classifier was added after seeing that the point forecasts had almost no skill, and is reported regardless of its result. Intervals: CQR was named as the primary method before the test run; split conformal is reported alongside it. The linear model underperformed and is reported as is.

Reproduce

pip install -r requirements.txt
python run_all.py
